svg.text: 4-pin stack bus (owner, 2026-11-16): power plus one RS-485 pair, passed straight through every module. Connector part and pitch: D-9. Protocol details will be
Draft C.9 · 2026-11-19 · PRD 0.5 · prices at 100 units

g.text: 5–32 V stack supply, fed by any module (PWR-4)
• Each module drives the bus from a spare UART through a small RS-485 transceiver (≈ INR 26). No extra processor on
the Fieldbus controller, Wi-Fi + BLE or LoRa module.
• The elected coordinator (Fieldbus controller > Wi-Fi + BLE > LoRa, SYS-5) only hands out transmit turns, about
every 20 ms, so only one module transmits at a time.
• Discovery by each MCU's unique ID; no address switches. Type, hardware revision, serial and firmware version are
• Load: the shared IO image is about 0.1 Mbit/s. Bulk 4G traffic uses the 4G card's own RJ45.
• 4G card: the modem has no MCU of ours, so how it joins the bus is open — D-29 (recommended: a small bus-bridge MCU
• Why not I3C or CAN-FD: I3C exists only on the STM32H5 and is a short on-board bus; the ESP32-C6 has classic CAN
only and the STM32WLE5 has no CAN.
What the 40-pin bus did — and what replaces it
discovery by unique ID; slot order not known
published in the module's next turn, ≤ ≈ 20 ms
each MCU's own watchdog; reset command over the bus
power-fail message from the battery host
one bus cycle ≈ 20 ms: every module gets one turn; every frame is heard by every module
• In its turn a module publishes frames tagged with a topic (for example io/fc/di). Every module hears every frame
on the shared pair and keeps only the topics it subscribes to — no relaying through a hub.
• Same model inside each module: Zephyr zbus channels, with selected channels bridged onto the bus; the coordinator
maps bus topics to MQTT topics for the cloud.
• Every frame carries a sequence number, CRC and a message authentication code with the stack key handed out by the
coordinator (SEC-5); output commands are accepted only from the configured owner (IO-6).
Power stage — on every module PCB (PWR-10, ≈ INR 85)
4-pin bus through every bridge plug: BUS_V · GND · RS485_A · RS485_B
Battery + charger board — optional, one per module (PWR-2)
TI BQ25601 charger, power path, 5 V
• Mains lost: the BQ25601 power path keeps the cell connected and its boost drives the module's 5 V rail without a dropout; a
module with a battery can also feed BUS_V. Each module broadcasts a power-fail message on the bus.
• Every module is also a standalone product, so each can take its own battery board (owner, 2026-11-19). In a stack, charging is
capped at 0.3 A per board so one 12 V 18 W adapter is enough (PWR-3).
• Current through the first bridge carries the whole stack: about 0.83 A at 24 V, 1.67 A at 12 V, 2.22 A at 9 V. Prefer
a 24 V bus; at most 4 modules on a 9 V supply.
• Power budget (R06, to be recomputed for the 12 V adapter and the integrated 4G module): about 9 W average, 15–20 W
peak for a full stack; the 4G module alone peaks near 10.6 W, about 5 W at the bus with local buffering. The external
adapter is 12 V 18 W: a 4-module stack needs ≈ 13–14 W with charging capped at 0.3 A per battery board.
• The bus is not hot-pluggable. The exposed connector on the end module gets a cap and ESD protection (EMC-3); the bus
• Only power and one RS-485 pair cross the bus; each module's Ethernet, USB and radios stay local.
• Li-ion: cells to IEC 62133-2 / UN 38.3 and BIS IS 16046-2; charging only between 0 and 45 °C, blocked in hot cabinets.
• A power-fail message gives every module early warning to save state and send a last-gasp message.
• 4G module: modem bursts (up to about 2 A at 3.8 V) come from ≥ 1000 µF on its 3.8 V rail behind a current-limited
buck, so the bus sees a smooth current (PWR-8). Its power stage must pass about 0.9 A at 12 V.
• The supply is never mains: a separate certified 12 V adapter is supplied (PWR-3); relay contacts may switch mains
loads, isolated by 5 kV from the electronics. With it the bus runs at 12 V (about 1.67 A through the first bridge at
